unit.unitOverview: Report what people said without taking their side or yours. Turn a question into a reported one, tell a request from an instruction, and choose a reporting verb you could defend if challenged. Then disagree at the right strength, and give reasons, aims and examples in language that belongs in a written record.
unit.learningPath:
The lesson: listen first, then read it back.
Words: five groups, 29 words. Listen and say each one.
Patterns: 5 cards. Read the one done for you before you try.
Reading: two records of one meeting, a language guide and a set of minutes.
Questions: 10 about the three texts.
Speaking: tap the mic, say it, listen back.
Writing: four tasks, each with a model.
Practice and the check: 7 exercises, then 12 questions.
functions: Write down what somebody asked, without quoting them
Report a request as a request, not as an order
Report somebody fairly, even when you disagree with them
Disagree with somebody senior without causing offence
Say whether something is forbidden or merely optional
Agree to most of a proposal and name what you do not agree to
Give a reason, an aim and an example in formal writing

visual.lectureScript:
This unit is about reporting what other people said, and about disagreeing with them.
Those two things belong together, because the moment you disagree with somebody you have to say what they said first, and how you say it decides everything that follows.

The reading opens with something that really happens in offices.
Two people wrote up the same meeting. One record said the supplier STATED that the part had been faulty. The other said he CLAIMED it.
Nobody changed a single fact. One word did all of it.
Stated is neutral. Claimed tells the reader not to believe him, before they have read anything else.
Hold on to that, because the third pattern in this unit is entirely about it.

The first pattern fills a real gap.
Level 2 showed you how to report a statement and how to report a command.
She said that it was ready. She told me to wait.
It never showed you how to report a QUESTION, and that is the first card.
The trick is one you already own, from Unit 4.
The question goes back into statement order.
Where is the file becomes she asked where the file WAS.
What does it cost becomes he asked what it COST, and the does vanishes.
And if there is no question word, because it was a yes-or-no question, you need whether or if.
Have you finished becomes she asked WHETHER I had finished.
One more thing. There is no question mark. A reported question is a statement about a question, not a question.

The second pattern is a distinction that matters more than it looks.
Level 2 gave you she told me to wait. That reports an instruction, from somebody who could give one.
But if a colleague says could you wait a moment, she ASKED you. She could have been refused.
Reporting that as she told me to wait puts authority in her hands that she did not have.
In ordinary conversation nobody would care. In a complaint, in a grievance, in minutes read by people who were not there, that is the whole difference.
The test is simple. Could the person have said no? If yes, it was a request.
And there is a family of these verbs, each carrying its own force. Warned. Reminded. Urged. Advised. Persuaded.
She warned me not to sign it says there was a danger. She reminded me to sign it says I already knew. Choosing the verb is choosing what you are saying happened.

Which brings us to the third pattern, and this is the one worth the most.
Level 2 treated every reporting verb as neutral. Most of them are not.
Said and stated take no position. Claimed and alleged tell the reader to doubt. Admitted and acknowledged say the speaker gave ground against their own interest. Insisted says they were pushed and did not move. Denied says they rejected it outright.
Before you write a loaded one, ask yourself one question. Can I support this?
If you write claimed about somebody who was telling the truth, you have not reported them. You have accused them, and a reader who knows the facts will notice.
The same runs the other way. Writing she admitted the work was finished is wrong if finishing the work helped her, because admitted means it cost her something.

The fourth pattern is about strength.
You have met most of these modals already, across five cards in Levels 1 and 2, one at a time.
What nobody has done is line them up.
That may not be the whole picture. I might be missing something, but. I am not sure that is right. I do not think that is right. That is not right.
Five ways to say one thing, and they cost you very different amounts.
The skill is picking the softest rung that still says what you mean, because you can always go up and it is very hard to come back down.
There is one pair in here to be careful with, and the reading in this unit is about it.
You must not sign it means signing is forbidden.
You need not sign it means signing is optional.
One word apart, opposite meanings. And the reason it catches people is that must is the exception: with can and should, adding not negates the whole sentence, but must not attacks the action rather than the obligation.

The last pattern gives you four connectives that do work because and so cannot.
As and since give a reason the reader already knows, where because usually gives news.
Therefore gives the result, formally, and it takes a full stop because it is an adverb.
Such as introduces examples, and never needs etc. after it, because such as already means among others.
And so that gives the PURPOSE, which is the one worth slowing down for.
We photographed it so that we had a record means having a record was the aim.
We photographed it, so we had a record means that is what happened to follow.
Both are correct sentences. Only one of them says you were thinking ahead.
Start with the words. Say each one aloud before you move on.

readings.title: Two Versions of the Same Meeting
readings.setting: An office, a week after the meeting
readings.passageScript:
I wrote the minutes and somebody else wrote a summary, and the two read like different meetings.
Mine said the supplier stated that the part had been faulty on arrival.
The other said the supplier claimed the part had been faulty on arrival.
Nobody changed a single fact. One word did all of it.
Stated is neutral. Claimed tells the reader not to believe him, before they have read anything else.
As it happens, I think he was probably wrong. But we had no evidence either way at that point.
Writing claimed put a judgement into a record that was supposed to hold only what was said.
The second thing I noticed was the requests.
The summary said the manager told the supplier to re-test the batch.
She did not tell him anything. She asked, and he could have said no, and for a while it looked as though he would.
Told makes it an instruction from somebody with authority over him. She had none.
Since the minutes may be read by people who were not there, both of those matter.
A record is not neutral because you meant it to be. It is neutral because you chose the verbs carefully.

readings.title: Must Not and Need Not
readings.setting: A page from a language guide
readings.passageScript:
Two phrases in English are one word apart and mean opposite things.
You must not sign it means signing is forbidden.
You need not sign it means signing is optional.
The mistake is easy to make and the consequences are not small.
There is a reason it catches people out.
In most pairs, adding not to the modal negates the whole sentence.
You can go becomes you cannot go. You should go becomes you should not go.
But must works differently. Must not negates the ACTION, not the obligation.
The way to remember it is to ask which word the not is attacking.
In you must not sign, the not attacks signing. Signing is what is forbidden.
In you need not sign, the not attacks the need. The need is what is absent.
Do not have to behaves like need not, not like must not.
You do not have to sign means the same as you need not sign.
If you are ever unsure in writing, avoid both and say it plainly.
Signing is not required. Do not sign this form. Neither of those can be misread.

grammar.title: She asked whether I had finished: reporting a question
grammar.explanation:
Level 2 showed you how to report a STATEMENT and a COMMAND.
She said that it was ready. She told me to wait.
It never showed you how to report a QUESTION, and that is this card.
The trick is one you have already met, in a different place.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
The question goes back into STATEMENT order, exactly as in a polite question.

Direct:   'Where is the file?'
Reported: She asked where the file WAS.

Direct:   'What does it cost?'
Reported: He asked what it COST.   (does disappears)

A yes-or-no question needs IF or WHETHER:
Direct:   'Have you finished?'
Reported: She asked whether I had finished.

The verb usually steps one tense back:
is -> was      does -> did      have -> had      will -> would

And the pronouns move with the speaker:
'Have YOU finished?' -> She asked whether I had finished.

No question mark, because a reported question is a statement about a question.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
Report this: She said, 'What does it cost?'
1. Choose the reporting verb: asked, because it was a question.
2. Keep the question word: what.
3. Put the inside back into statement order: it costs.
4. Step the tense back: costs becomes cost. The does disappears.
5. No question mark: the whole sentence is a statement now.
Answer: She asked what it cost.
grammar.commonMistake:
Learners keep the question order, exactly as they do with polite questions.
No: She asked where was the file.
Yes: She asked where the file was.
It is the same rule you met with Could you tell me where the venue is.
grammar.memoryTip: A reported question is a statement. Statement order, no question mark.

grammar.reviewStatus: Script review and curriculum sign-off pending
grammar.title: Told me to, or asked me to: the difference is who had the power
grammar.explanation:
Level 2 gave you one of these: she told me to wait.
That reports an instruction from somebody who could give one.
A request is different, and reporting it with tell changes the story.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
TELL somebody TO do something — an instruction, from somebody with authority.
She told me to wait.
He told them not to sign it.

ASK somebody TO do something — a request, which could have been refused.
She asked me to wait.
He asked them not to sign it.

Both take: verb + person + TO + plain verb.
The negative puts NOT before the to:
She asked me NOT TO sign it.

Neither takes that:
NOT: She asked me that I wait.

Other verbs in the same shape, each carrying its own force:
advised, warned, reminded, persuaded, urged, invited, ordered
She warned me not to sign it.  (a danger)
She reminded me to sign it.    (I already knew)
She urged me to sign it.       (strongly, repeatedly)

Choosing the verb is choosing what you are alleging happened.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
Report this, given that she had no authority over you: 'Please wait,' she said.
1. Was it an instruction or a request? A request — she could not order you.
2. A request is reported with ask, not tell.
3. The shape is ask + person + to + plain verb.
Answer: She asked me to wait.
She told me to wait would report her as having authority she did not have.
grammar.commonMistake:
Reporting a request as an instruction quietly changes who was in charge.
If your colleague says please could you check this, she asked you to check it.
She told me to check it says something different about the relationship,
and in a complaint or a grievance that difference matters.
grammar.memoryTip: tell reports an instruction. ask reports a request. Choose by who could refuse.
grammar.practice:

4. Your manager: 'Do not sign it.'
5. A colleague: 'Do not forget to sign it.' (you already knew)
6. A friend, repeatedly: 'You really should apply.'
Now correct these.
7. She asked me that I wait.
8. She asked me to not sign it.
grammar.answerKey:
1. My manager told me to wait here.
2. A colleague asked me to wait a moment.
3. A friend warned me not to sign it.
4. My manager told me not to sign it.
5. A colleague reminded me to sign it.
6. A friend urged me to apply.
7. She asked me to wait. (ask never takes that in this shape)
8. She asked me not to sign it. (not goes BEFORE to)
6 or more right: good.

grammar.reviewStatus: Script review and curriculum sign-off pending
grammar.title: He claimed, she admitted: the verb that passes judgement
grammar.explanation:
Level 2 treated every reporting verb as neutral: said, told.
Most of them are not. The verb you choose tells the reader what YOU think
of what was said, before they have read a word of it.
In a report or a complaint this is the most loaded choice you make.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
NEUTRAL — you take no position:
said, stated, told me, explained, mentioned

DOUBTING — you are signalling that it may not be true:
claimed, alleged, maintained
He claimed the part was faulty on arrival.
(the reader now expects it was not)

CONCEDING — the speaker gave ground, against their own interest:
admitted, accepted, acknowledged, conceded
She admitted the invoice had been sent late.

INSISTING — the speaker was pushed and did not move:
insisted, maintained, contended

DENYING — the speaker rejected it:
denied, disputed, rejected
Note: denied takes -ing, not that + to.
He denied sending it. / He denied that he had sent it.

The test before you write one: can you support the judgement?
Writing claimed about somebody who was telling the truth is not neutral reporting.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
You are writing a complaint. The supplier said the part was faulty when it
arrived. You have a photograph showing it was not. Which verb?
1. Do you accept what was said? No, and you have evidence.
2. A doubting verb signals that to the reader.
3. claimed is the standard one.
Answer: The supplier claimed the part was faulty on arrival.
Then give the photograph. The verb prepares the reader; the evidence does the work.
grammar.commonMistake:
A doubting verb with no evidence behind it reads as unfair, and it weakens you.
Weak: He claimed he had posted it. (if you have no reason to doubt him)
Better: He said he had posted it.
Save claimed for when you can show why.
grammar.memoryTip: The verb is your judgement. Only use a loaded one when you can back it.
grammar.practice:

2. She gave ground against her own interest. She ___ the invoice was late.
3. You take no position at all. He ___ the office closes at five.
4. He was challenged twice and did not move. He ___ he had never been told.
5. He rejected the accusation outright. He ___ sending it.
6. She agreed to one narrow part only. She ___ the delay, but not the cost.
Now decide whether each is fair.
7. He claimed he had posted it. (you have no reason to doubt him)
8. She admitted the work was finished. (it was, and it helped her)
grammar.answerKey:
1. claimed  2. admitted (or conceded)  3. said (or stated)
4. maintained (or insisted)  5. denied  6. acknowledged
7. Unfair. Use said. claimed accuses him with nothing behind it.
8. Wrong verb. admitted implies it cost her something, and it did not. Use said or confirmed.
7 and 8 are the judgement the card is teaching.
6 or more right: good.

grammar.title: May, might, could: disagreeing without a row
grammar.explanation:
You have met most of these modals already, one at a time, across five cards
in Levels 1 and 2. What no card has done is line them up by STRENGTH.
Disagreeing well is almost entirely a matter of picking the right rung.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
SAYING SOMEBODY IS WRONG, from softest to hardest:
That may not be the whole picture.
I might be missing something, but ...
I am not sure that is right.
I do not think that is right.
That is not right.
All five say the same thing. They cost you very different amounts.

SUGGESTING, softest first:
We could look at it again.
We might want to look at it again.
Perhaps we should look at it again.
We need to look at it again.
We must look at it again.

OBLIGATION AND PROHIBITION, which you already have:
must / have to      an obligation
must not            a prohibition
need not / do not have to   no obligation (NOT a prohibition)

The pair learners confuse, and it matters:
You must not sign it.   = signing is forbidden
You need not sign it.   = signing is optional
Opposite meanings, one word apart.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
Your manager states a figure you believe is wrong, in front of other people.
1. Ask what it costs to be blunt here. A lot: it is public, and they are senior.
2. So choose a soft rung, and leave yourself room to be wrong.
3. Add a reason, because a soft disagreement with no reason is just doubt.
Answer: I might be missing something, but I had a different figure for March.
That is not right may be true and buys you nothing you needed.
grammar.commonMistake:
must not and need not are one word apart and mean opposite things.
You must not sign it = do NOT sign.
You need not sign it = you may sign or not, as you like.
Getting this wrong in writing has real consequences.
grammar.memoryTip: Pick the softest rung that still says what you mean. You can always go up.
grammar.practice:

7. That is wrong.
8. You have to do it again.
grammar.answerKey:
1. might  2. must not  3. need not  4. could  5. must (or have to)  6. may
7. I am not sure that is right. / That may not be the whole picture.
8. We might want to look at it again. / It could be worth doing again.
Numbers 2 and 3 are the pair that mean opposite things.
6 or more right: good.

grammar.reviewStatus: Script review and curriculum sign-off pending
grammar.title: As, therefore, so that, such as: four ways to explain
grammar.explanation:
You have because and so, from Level 1 and Level 2.
Those two cover most of daily speech and almost none of formal writing.
These four each do a job because and so cannot do.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
AS and SINCE — the reason, given first, when it is already known.
As the part was still under guarantee, we returned it.
Since nobody had signed for it, we could not trace it.
because usually gives NEW information; as and since give known information.

THEREFORE — the result, formally. It is an adverb, so it takes a full stop.
The part was under guarantee. Therefore we returned it.

SO THAT — the PURPOSE, not the result. It answers what for.
We photographed it so that we had a record.
Compare: We photographed it, so we had a record. (that is a result)
so that = in order to. so = and as a result.

SUCH AS — examples, introducing a list you are not finishing.
Several items were missing, such as the seal and the bracket.
like does the same job and is less formal.
Do not use etc. with such as: such as already means among others.
grammar.workedExample:
One done, step by step.
Choose: We photographed it ___ we had a record.
1. Ask what the second half is. Is it what happened, or what you were aiming at?
2. Having a record was the AIM. You photographed it in order to get one.
3. Purpose takes so that.
Answer: We photographed it so that we had a record.
With so alone it would read as a result: we photographed it, and as it turned out,
that gave us a record. True, but not what you meant.
grammar.commonMistake:
so and so that look almost identical and answer different questions.
so = and as a result (what happened next)
so that = in order that (what you were aiming at)
If you can replace it with in order to, you need so that.
grammar.memoryTip: because gives news. as gives what they already know. so that gives the aim.

grammar.answerKey:
1. so that  2. so  3. As  4. Therefore  5. such as  6. Since
7. We kept a copy so that we had proof if needed.
8. Items were missing, such as the seal and the bracket. (such as already means among others)
Numbers 1 and 2 are the pair: the aim, against what happened.

assignments.title: Minutes, and then the disagreement
assignments.instructions:
Part one. Write five numbered minutes of a meeting you invent, in about 130 words.
Include at least one reported question, one request, one concession and one dispute.
Use at least five different reporting verbs, and beside each one, in brackets, write
three words saying why that verb is defensible.
Part two. You disagree with one thing decided in that meeting.
Write the disagreement five times, softest to hardest, then say which you would send
and to whom.
Part three. Write four sentences about the same incident using as, therefore, so that
and such as, each once.
Nothing in part one may contain an opinion of your own.
